What the official sources say

  • A summary proceeding to remove a person may be maintained after a ten-day notice to quit where the respondent has intruded into or squatted upon the property without permission and occupancy continued without permission or permission was revoked and notice given. (RPAPL § 713(3); source)
  • A licensee whose license has expired or been revoked, or whose licensor is no longer entitled to possession, may be removed by summary proceeding after a ten-day notice to quit. (RPAPL § 713(7); source)

New York Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession FAQ

Can a squatter take ownership of my New York house?

Check the statute and talk to a New York attorney about your facts.

Can a squatter take ownership of a New York house?

Only by adverse possession, and the statute makes that hard. Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law section 501 says an adverse possessor gains title when the ten-year period in CPLR 212(a) runs out, provided the occupancy was adverse, under a claim of right, open and notorious, continuous, exclusive and actual.

The statute ties title to the end of the ten years, so an owner who finds someone living in a vacant or inherited house should treat it as urgent. Each element is something the occupier has to establish, and a missing one defeats the claim.

What does a squatter have to prove in New York?

The occupier has to show each statutory element, and the court looks at the facts of the occupancy. The Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law breaks the claim into pieces:

  • Adverse possessor. Someone who occupies another person's real property, with or without knowing about the owner's superior rights, in a way that would give the owner a cause of action for ejectment (section 501(1)).
  • Claim of right. A reasonable basis for believing the property belongs to the occupier. The requirement falls away if the owners cannot be found in the county clerk or register records and located by reasonable means (section 501(3)).
  • Possession without a written instrument. The land must have been occupied through acts open enough to put a reasonably diligent owner on notice, or protected by a substantial enclosure (section 522).
  • Possession under a deed or judgment. Ten years of continued possession under a written conveyance or a court decree, with a separate rule that holding one lot in a divided tract is not holding the others (section 511).

When a claim rests on a written instrument or judgment, section 512 adds a third path: land not enclosed that was used for fuel or fencing timber for farming or the occupant's ordinary needs.

Why does the ten-year period matter to an owner?

The ten years come from CPLR section 212(a), which bars an action to recover real property or its possession unless the plaintiff or a predecessor was seized or possessed of the premises within the previous ten years. A house that sits empty for a long time, often after the owner has died, is where that clock does its damage.

The test in section 522 asks whether acts were open enough to put a reasonably diligent owner on notice. Heirs who inherit a house they do not plan to live in should have someone check it on a regular schedule until it is sold.

How does an owner remove someone who has no right to be there?

Through a court proceeding. Section 711 of the Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law, found on the Senate's statute page, defines a squatter as a person who enters onto or intrudes upon property without permission and continues to occupy it without title, right or permission. It says a tenant does not include a squatter, and that no tenant or lawful occupant can be removed except through a special proceeding.

Where the squatter rules and section 713(3) conflict, section 713 controls. That section allows a special proceeding after a ten-day notice to quit when someone has intruded on or squatted upon the property without the owner's permission and the occupancy has continued, or permission was revoked and notice given. Section 713 lists other grounds that apply where no landlord-tenant relationship exists:

Grounds for removal where no landlord-tenant relationship exists (source: RPAPL section 713)
SubdivisionSituationNotice
713(3)Squatter, or permission revoked with noticeTen-day notice to quit
713(5)Property sold in foreclosure, deed shown to the occupantTen-day notice to quit
713(7)Licensee whose license expired, was revoked, or whose licensor lost the right to possessTen-day notice to quit
713(8)Former owner who sold to a purchaser for value and stays on without permissionTen-day notice to quit
713(10)Entry or holding by force or unlawful means, where the petitioner was in peaceful possessionNone required

What is the force or unlawful entry route?

Subdivision 10 of section 713 lets the owner proceed without a notice to quit when the occupant entered or remains by force or unlawful means. Two conditions apply: the occupant or a predecessor was not in quiet possession for three years before the forcible or unlawful entry, and the petitioner was peaceably in actual possession when the entry happened, or in constructive possession at the time of an unlawful holding.

That wording means the facts matter a great deal. An owner who left a house vacant and returned to find strangers inside should write down when the house was last occupied by the owner, what locks and fences were in place, and when the occupants were first seen. A New York attorney can say which subdivision fits those facts.

What happens if an owner tries to lock someone out?

A self-help lockout can turn the owner into the defendant. Section 768 makes it unlawful to evict, or try to evict, a person who has lawfully occupied a dwelling for thirty consecutive days or longer, or who holds a lease, except under a warrant or court order. The prohibited conduct includes:

  • using or threatening force to make the occupant leave;
  • cutting off essential services;
  • removing the occupant's belongings or the entrance door;
  • changing or disabling the lock without giving the occupant a key.

An intentional violation is a class A misdemeanor, and each violation can also bring a civil penalty of $1,000 to $10,000. Separately, section 853 lets a person who is put out of property in a forcible or unlawful way recover treble damages from the wrongdoer.

Whether someone is a lawful occupant, a licensee or a squatter can be a contested question. Do not change locks or remove belongings until an attorney has said the proceeding is complete.

How does a squatter issue affect selling a New York house?

An occupant with a claim to the property will show up in the buyer's due diligence and can delay a closing. Tell the title company and the closing attorney about any person living in the house who is not the seller, and ask whether a proceeding under article 7 is needed before delivery of possession.

A seller who has already started a special proceeding should share its status with any buyer. If an occupant is a family member, a former tenant or a person the owner once allowed to stay, the right removal ground may be different from the squatter rule, so describe the history accurately.

Owners of a vacant inherited house can also look at probate. Letters from the Surrogate's Court give a fiduciary the authority to manage the property and, unless the will or court says otherwise, to sell it. Our New York probate guide covers that process.

More questions about New York Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession

How many years does adverse possession take in New York?

Ten years. Section 501 ties title to the expiration of the CPLR 212(a) limitations period, and the occupancy must have been adverse, under claim of right, open and notorious, continuous, exclusive and actual throughout. Missing any element defeats the claim.

Can I just change the locks on a squatter?

Not safely. Section 768 makes it a class A misdemeanor to evict or try to evict an occupant of thirty consecutive days or longer without a court order, and changing a lock without giving the occupant a key is listed as prohibited conduct. Whether the person is a squatter is a legal question for a court.

What notice does a New York owner give a squatter?

A ten-day notice to quit under section 713, served as section 735 requires, before a special proceeding for someone who intruded without permission. Where the occupant entered by force or unlawful means, subdivision 10 says no notice to quit is required. A lawyer should choose the ground.

Does paying property tax give a squatter title in New York?

The sections reviewed here do not list tax payment among the elements. Title depends on ten years of adverse, open, continuous, exclusive and actual occupancy under a claim of right, or the written instrument and judgment rules. Ask an attorney how tax payments might be used on your facts.

Can a squatter be a tenant under New York law?

No. Section 711 says a tenant does not include a squatter, and defines a squatter as someone who enters without permission and stays without title, right or permission. Someone who has permission, such as a licensee or tenant, is handled under different grounds.

New York Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • No security deposit or advance may exceed one month's rent (non-rent-stabilized dwellings). (General Obligations Law § 7-108(1-a)(a); source)
  • On conveyance of leased premises, the grantee is also liable to the tenant for repayment of the security deposit if the grantee had actual knowledge of it; knowledge is deemed for deposits in a bank within six months before closing or acknowledged in a lease in effect at closing. (GOL § 7-105 / 7-108 (sale of premises provisions); source)
  • Notice of rent increase of 5% or more or non-renewal: at least 30 days if tenant occupied less than one year; 60 days if one to two years; 90 days if more than two years (or lease term of at least two years). (Real Property Law § 226-c; source)
  • Landlord is deemed to warrant that premises and common areas are fit for human habitation and for the uses reasonably intended by the parties. (Real Property Law § 235-b; source)

Get My Cash Offer →

How much can a New York landlord collect as a security deposit?

One month's rent is the ceiling for most dwellings. General Obligations Law section 7-108(1-a) bars any deposit or advance above that amount, with carve-outs for seasonal units, owner-occupied co-op apartments and a few other housing types such as assisted living. The rule applies in the statute to non-rent-stabilized units and cannot be waived in a lease.

The whole deposit comes back to the tenant on move-out, less reasonable and itemized costs for unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear, unpaid utilities owed to the landlord and moving or storage of belongings. Ordinary wear and damage left by a prior tenant cannot be charged.

  • Before move-in, the landlord must offer a walk-through with the tenant, and if the tenant asks, both sign a written condition report.
  • Before move-out, the landlord must tell the tenant of the right to an inspection, held one to two weeks before the tenancy ends, with 48 hours' written notice.
  • Within 14 days after the tenant leaves, the landlord must send an itemized statement and the balance. Miss that deadline and the right to keep any part of the deposit is gone.
  • In a dispute the landlord has to prove the amount kept was reasonable, and a willful violation can bring punitive damages up to twice the deposit.

Who is responsible for the tenant's deposit when a landlord sells?

The buyer can end up owing it. If the old landlord does not hand the deposit over, section 7-108(2) makes the new owner liable for the deposit plus interest whenever the buyer had actual knowledge of it. Knowledge is presumed in three situations.

When a buyer is treated as knowing about a tenant deposit, General Obligations Law 7-108(2)
SituationWhat follows
Deposit placed in a bank in the six months before closingBuyer is deemed to know of it
Deposit acknowledged in a lease in effect at closingBuyer is deemed to know of it
Tenant supplies a cancelled check, receipt or signed lease from a prior ownerBuyer is deemed to know of it
No record of a deposit anywhereBuyer must send written notice within 30 days after closing, and the tenant has 30 days to show proof

Source: New York State Senate, Open Legislation.

A buyer who finds no record can demand that the seller set up an escrow account equal to one month's rent to cover a late claim. Sellers who keep clean deposit records and give the buyer copies at closing avoid that argument entirely.

How much notice must a landlord give for a rent increase or non-renewal?

When the rent goes up by 5 percent or more, or the landlord will not renew, written notice is required, and its length depends on how long the tenant has lived there. Real Property Law section 226-c sets 30 days for under one year of occupancy, 60 days for one to two years and 90 days for more than two years or a lease of at least two years. The longer of the tenant's total time in the home or the length of the lease governs.

If a landlord gives late notice, the tenancy continues on its existing terms from the day written notice arrives until the full notice period has run. Under the version in force until June 15, 2034, the notice must also say whether the unit falls under Article 6-A, the good cause eviction law, and if it is exempt, why.

Section 214 lists the exemptions. They include owner-occupied buildings with no more than ten units, small landlords who disclose their ownership, condominium and cooperative units, rent-regulated units and homes with a certificate of occupancy issued on or after January 1, 2009 for thirty years. Section 214 also refers to local laws adopted by villages, towns and cities outside New York City, so ask the local clerk whether yours has one.

What does the warranty of habitability require?

Every residential lease, written or oral, carries an implied promise from the landlord that the home and the common areas are fit to live in. Real Property Law section 235-b says occupants may not be subjected to conditions dangerous, hazardous or harmful to life, health or safety, and any waiver by the tenant is void.

  • A condition caused by the tenant or someone under the tenant's direction is not a breach.
  • A court assessing damages does not need expert testimony.
  • For rent-regulated homes, damages are reduced by any rent reduction already ordered by the state housing agency for the same problem.

For a seller, the warranty applies to every residential lease in the building, so open repair complaints are worth sorting out before listing.

Can a landlord evict without going to court?

No. Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law section 711 says no tenant or lawful occupant of a dwelling may be removed except in a special proceeding. The same section defines a squatter as a person who enters or stays on property without the owner's permission or any right, and says a squatter is not a tenant.

The common grounds are a tenant staying after the lease ends and a tenant who has defaulted on rent. For unpaid rent, the landlord must serve a written demand giving at least 14 days to pay or leave, and the notice must follow the service rules in section 735. Until June 15, 2034, that notice also has to carry the Article 6-A disclosure described above.

Two smaller duties often come up in nonpayment cases. Under section 235-e, a landlord taking cash or any payment other than the tenant's personal check must give a written receipt with the date, amount, premises and period covered, and signature and title. If rent is not received within five days of the due date, the landlord must send a notice by certified mail, and skipping it is an affirmative defense for the tenant in a nonpayment case.

Does a tenant who moves out early still owe rent?

Often the answer is partly. Real Property Law section 227-e requires a landlord whose tenant leaves in breach of the lease to act in good faith and take reasonable, customary steps to re-rent at fair market value or the old rent, whichever is lower. When a new tenant's lease starts, it ends the earlier lease and reduces what the first tenant owes.

The party asking for damages carries the burden of proof, and a lease clause that excuses the landlord from mitigating is void as against public policy. A landlord who is also thinking about selling should keep records of advertising and showings, since they are the evidence a court will want.

How should an owner prepare to sell a New York rental?

Start with paper. Gather every lease, the deposit records and the dates of the last rent notices, because the buyer's attorney will ask for them and a buyer can be liable for any deposit it knew about. Check rent receipts, since a gap in receipts can matter if a nonpayment case follows.

  • Confirm whether any unit is rent-regulated or exempt from the good cause law, and note the reason.
  • Do not try to remove a tenant yourself. A special proceeding in court is required.
  • Time any non-renewal or rent notice to the 30, 60 or 90 day schedule so it does not become an argument at closing.
  • Resolve habitability complaints in writing, since they carry over to the buyer.

Rent-regulated homes follow separate laws, which the statutes name as the rent stabilization law, the city rent and rehabilitation law and the emergency housing rent control law. Ask your attorney which regime covers your building.

More questions about New York Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights

What is the maximum security deposit in New York?

One month's rent for most dwellings. The cap comes from General Obligations Law section 7-108(1-a), which lists exceptions such as seasonal units and owner-occupied co-op apartments.

How fast must a landlord return a deposit?

Within 14 days after the tenant has moved out, with an itemized statement of any deductions. A landlord who misses the deadline gives up the right to keep any part of it.

How much notice is needed for a New York rent increase?

For an increase of 5 percent or more, 30 days if the tenant has lived there under a year, 60 days for one to two years and 90 days beyond that, under Real Property Law section 226-c.

Can a buyer be held liable for a deposit the seller kept?

Yes, when the buyer had actual knowledge of it. Deposits in a bank within six months of closing or named in a lease then in force count as known to the buyer.

Who counts as a squatter in New York?

A person who enters or stays on property with no permission, title or right. Under RPAPL section 711, a squatter is not a tenant, though a lawful tenant can only be removed through a special proceeding.

New York Probate Laws: Who Inherits, Small Estates and Selling the House

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Spouse and issue: $50,000 and one-half of the residue to the spouse, balance to issue by representation. (EPTL § 4-1.1(a)(1); source)
  • Spouse and no issue: the whole to the spouse. (EPTL § 4-1.1(a)(2); source)
  • Issue and no spouse: the whole to the issue by representation. (EPTL § 4-1.1(a)(3); source)
  • A small estate is one leaving personal property with gross value of $50,000 or less (excluding EPTL 5-3.1(a) set-off property); handled by voluntary administration. (SCPA § 1301; source)
Selling in New York?
We buy New York houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Who inherits a New York house when there is no will?

Under Estates, Powers and Trusts Law section 4-1.1, the order of inheritance runs from the spouse and children outward through parents, siblings, grandparents and more distant relatives. The share comes after debts, administration expenses and reasonable funeral costs are subtracted.

Intestate distribution in New York (source: EPTL section 4-1.1(a))
SurvivorsWho takes the estate
Spouse and children or other issue$50,000 and half of the rest to the spouse, the balance to the issue
Spouse, no issueAll to the spouse
Issue, no spouseAll to the issue, by representation
Parents onlyAll to the surviving parent or parents
Issue of parents onlyAll to those siblings and their issue
Grandparents or their issue onlySplit by paternal and maternal side

Half-blood relatives are treated as whole-blood relatives. A child conceived before the death and born alive afterward inherits as if born during the decedent's life. The spouse's share is in place of any right of dower.

What is a small estate in New York?

A small estate is one where the decedent left personal property with a gross value of $50,000 or less, not counting property set off for the family under EPTL 5-3.1(a). Surrogate's Court Procedure Act section 1301 defines it that way, and such an estate can be settled by a voluntary administrator without formal court administration.

The definition counts personal property. A house is real property, so the safe course is to ask the Surrogate's Court clerk in the decedent's county whether the voluntary route fits an estate that includes real estate. Do not assume a $50,000 limit decides it.

Where the route is available, section 1304 keeps it light:

  • No waiting period after the death applies.
  • The voluntary administrator does not post a bond.
  • The applicant files an affidavit and a certified copy of the death certificate with the clerk of the court in the county where the decedent lived.
  • No court order or hearing is needed, and a short certificate from the court shows the person's authority to banks and others holding the decedent's property.

Who can act as a voluntary administrator?

The right goes first to the surviving adult spouse when there is no will, and if there is none or the spouse renounces, then in order to an adult child or grandchild, parent, sibling, niece or nephew, or aunt or uncle. Section 1303 then moves to a guardian or committee for a distributee who cannot act, and finally to the chief fiscal officer of the county in counties without a public administrator.

If there is a will, the named executor or alternate executor has the first right and acts by filing the will with the surrogate's court. When that person renounces or fails to qualify by filing the required affidavit within thirty days after the will is filed, an adult who could petition for letters of administration with will annexed may step in. No one outside those lists can serve.

Who gets letters of administration when there is no will?

The court follows a priority list set by section 1001, and letters go to distributees who are eligible and qualify in this order:

  • the surviving spouse;
  • the children;
  • the grandchildren;
  • either parent;
  • the brothers or sisters;
  • any other distributee, with preference to the one entitled to the largest share.

Equally entitled distributees can share the appointment. The court can also grant letters to a non-distributee, or to a trust company, when all eligible distributees file acknowledged consents. When no eligible person accepts, letters go to the public administrator or the county's chief fiscal officer, then to the petitioner at the court's discretion.

Relatives who do not agree on who should serve should talk to a New York probate attorney before filing. Ask the attorney who holds the authority to sign a deed before any listing goes up.

What if the will names no executor?

The court issues letters of administration with the will annexed, using the priority in section 1418. A sole beneficiary comes first, then one or more residuary beneficiaries, and then other people interested in the estate.

If no eligible person will accept, letters issue to the public administrator or, where there is none, the county treasurer. The court may then turn to the petitioner or someone it designates. Beneficiaries can also consent to the appointment of a person who is not a beneficiary, or of a trust company, if all eligible beneficiaries sign acknowledged consents.

Can an executor sell the house before probate is finished?

Sometimes. A named executor can ask for preliminary letters once a probate petition is filed and process has issued, under section 1412. Those letters give the powers of an administrator, with one limit: they do not allow paying a legacy or distributive share.

Unless the court or the will says otherwise, a preliminary executor may take possession of, manage and sell real property devised by the will. If the house is specifically devised to someone, it can be sold only with that devisee's written consent or by court order. The preliminary executor must give notice of the appointment to all parties who have appeared within ten days.

The court may limit the letters to certain assets, and may revoke them for unreasonable delay in the probate proceeding.

What can a New York fiduciary do with a house?

Absent contrary terms in the will or the court order, EPTL section 11-1.1 gives a fiduciary a broad list of powers over estate property. For a house, the ones that matter most are:

  • to take possession, collect rents and manage it;
  • to sell it at public or private sale, on terms the fiduciary believes most advantageous to the people interested, unless the property is specifically disposed of;
  • to lease it for up to three years, or up to ten for a trustee;
  • to grant an option to buy for up to six months;
  • to insure it and make ordinary repairs;
  • to sign deeds, contracts and other documents needed to administer the estate.

A power the will forbids can still be exercised with the surrogate's approval when needed for the purposes in SCPA 1902. The court may also authorize powers the statute does not list.

Does an inherited house trigger New York transfer tax?

Passing a house to an heir does not, because the Tax Department's transfer tax page says a conveyance does not include a transfer by devise, bequest or inheritance. A later sale by the estate or an heir is a conveyance like any other, with the base tax of $2 per $500 paid by the seller.

If that sale reaches $1 million or more, the buyer owes the additional mansion tax, and the seller becomes liable if the buyer does not pay. Ask the closing attorney to prepare the transfer tax return before the date of delivery, since it is due by the fifteenth day after the deed is delivered.

More questions about New York Probate Laws

How much does a spouse inherit in New York without a will?

It depends on who else survives. With children, the spouse takes $50,000 plus half of the remainder. With no children or other issue, the spouse takes everything. The calculation starts after debts, administration costs and reasonable funeral expenses are taken out.

Does a New York small estate include real estate?

The statutory definition looks at personal property of $50,000 or less, and the statute does not mention a house. Ask the Surrogate's Court clerk in the county where the decedent lived whether voluntary administration can reach your situation before relying on it.

Who can sign the deed on an inherited New York house?

The statutes give the power to sell to the fiduciary the court appoints, such as an executor or administrator. Preliminary letters can also carry that power when a probate petition is pending, with consent rules if the house was specifically devised.

Do I need a bond to administer a small estate in New York?

No, a voluntary administrator does not need to give a bond. The person files an affidavit and a certified death certificate with the clerk of the court in the decedent's county. A short certificate from the court then proves the authority to act.

What happens if no family member will serve as administrator?

Letters can issue to the public administrator or, in counties without one, to the chief fiscal officer of the county. The court may also appoint the petitioner or another person it designates. Consents from all eligible distributees can allow a trust company or a non-relative to serve.

New York Tax Deed and Tax Lien Sales: Process, Redemption and Selling First

What the official sources say

  • Persons with interests may file a claim under RPTL 1135 or Title 6 for a share of any surplus attributable to sale of a foreclosed parcel. (RPTL § 1136; source)
Selling in New York?
We buy New York houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

How does a New York tax foreclosure or tax lien sale work?

When property tax goes unpaid, a lien attaches and the owner gets a fixed period to pay it off. If the period ends without payment, the tax district can foreclose in court, and in some places it can also sell the lien to an investor. Real Property Tax Law Article 11 sets out these procedures for the tax districts that follow it, and a few counties and cities enforce under their own charters instead.

The article is organized into titles: redemption, foreclosure by proceeding in rem, a homeowner bill of rights, general provisions, sales of delinquent tax liens, and distribution of surplus. A tax district that uses the article can end up with title through a court judgment, which is why the dates in your notice matter.

A private sale before that judgment lets you keep any equity above the tax debt.

How long do you have to redeem the property?

The redemption period ends two years after the lien date. Under section 1110, you redeem by paying the enforcing officer the delinquent tax lien plus all legal charges on or before the last day.

  • A tax district can lengthen the period for residential or farm property to three or four years by local law, under section 1111.
  • A tax district can shorten it to one year for residential vacant and abandoned property that was placed on a vacant and abandoned roll or list before the taxes became delinquent.
  • If the published foreclosure notice names a later date, the redemption period runs to that later date.

The statute defines residential property as a one-, two- or three-family structure used only for residential purposes. Ask your county treasurer or city finance office which period your municipality has adopted and what date they list for your parcel.

What charges are added to the unpaid tax?

Legal charges are part of the delinquent tax, so they count toward the redemption amount. Section 1102 lists them: costs of mailing and publishing notices, interest and penalties, recording fees, the cost of appraising the parcel to measure any surplus, and costs of searching the public record and other reasonable foreclosure expenses.

For that last group, the statute treats a charge of up to $250 per parcel, or 2% of the taxes, interest and penalties, whichever is greater, as reasonable without further proof. A tax district can charge more if it shows the court the larger amount was needed. When an officer posts a notice on the property itself, a $100 charge is added to the parcel under section 1125.

What notices will an owner receive before foreclosure?

The enforcing officer must mail a notice of the foreclosure to each owner and to others whose interest appears in the public record, by both certified mail and first class mail. Under section 1125, the notice is treated as received unless both mailings come back within 45 days.

The notice warns that foreclosure will cost the owner the property and all rights in it, and states the last day to redeem. For a residential parcel, it comes with the homeowner warning notice from section 1144. That warning says:

  • You are at risk of losing your home, and you can call the Attorney General's Homeowner Protection Program hotline for free housing counseling or legal help.
  • If nothing is done within ninety days of the mailing, the tax district may start legal action.
  • You may remain in the home until a court orders you out, and the notice is not an eviction notice.
  • Seniors, people with physical disabilities and veterans may qualify for a partial exemption, and the local assessor's office has the details.

Section 1125 also puts a duty on you: if your address changes, tell the enforcing officer in writing, since a court can weigh your failure to do so if you later claim you got no notice.

What happens at the final judgment?

If you answer the petition and the court finds the answer has merit, the petition is dismissed for that parcel. If no answer is filed, the court awards possession to the tax district, and the enforcing officer deeds the property to the district or, if the officer asks and the court agrees, directly to another party. Once the deed is signed, every person who held a right, title, lien or equity of redemption in the parcel is barred from asserting it.

When the court orders a sale after an answer, the officer holds a public auction after notice runs once a week for at least three successive weeks in a local newspaper. Section 1136 also lets the tax district, before the parcel is conveyed to a third party, convey title back to the former owner on payment of the taxes, penalties, interest and other lawful charges, but that is a choice the district makes.

Can you get money back if the property sells for more than the tax debt?

Possibly. Section 1197 allows anyone who held a right, title, interest, lien or equity of redemption just before the foreclosure judgment to file a claim with the court for a share of surplus from a sale.

The statute limits those claims. Where the property sold at public sale, the price paid is accepted as full value. For residential property, if no former homeowner has filed by the time the report of sale is confirmed and surplus remains, the proceeding stays open for at least three years. After that, unclaimed surplus is treated as abandoned and goes to the tax district to reduce its levy, not to the state comptroller.

What is a tax lien sale and how is it different?

In a lien sale, the tax district sells the debt rather than the house. Section 1190 allows a district to contract to sell some or all of its delinquent liens to the state's municipal bond bank or to tax lien entities the bank creates.

The enforcing officer must mail a notice at least 30 days before the sale to the owner and to anyone with a declaration of interest on file. After the sale, the buyer of the lien holds the right to collect, may hire a collection agency, and can take partial payments or set up installment agreements. You then pay the purchaser, not the municipality. Payments are applied first to collection costs and attorneys' fees, then to accrued interest, and last to principal.

What does a county lien sale look like in practice?

Nassau County on Long Island shows the calendar. The Treasurer's Tax Records department collects delinquent county taxes, and for the towns of Hempstead, North Hempstead and Oyster Bay that includes both general and school taxes. Collection of unpaid school tax begins June 1 and general tax September 1 each year.

For the 2026 delinquent taxes, the Treasurer's page lists personal checks from June 1 to November 30, 2026, and credit card or electronic check payments from June 26, 2026 to January 31, 2027. The last day to pay before the lien sale is Wednesday, February 10, 2027 at 3:00 PM. Tax liens themselves cannot be paid online and need a bank cashier's check or cash, and checks are made out to the Nassau County Treasurer, whose office is at 1 West Street in Mineola.

Other counties and cities run their own schedules. Ask your county treasurer, city finance office or receiver of taxes for the lien date, the redemption deadline and a written payoff figure.

Should you sell the house before the tax district acts?

Often, because a sale before the redemption date pays the taxes from the proceeds and leaves you whatever remains. After a judgment, your claim shrinks to a share of surplus that the court has to adjudicate.

Start by asking the enforcing officer for the full amount needed to redeem, including legal charges, and the exact last day. If the house is occupied by a tenant or full of an inherited estate's belongings, a buyer who purchases as-is can move faster than a listed sale. Get any payoff in writing and give it to the closing attorney so the lien is satisfied at the table.

More questions about New York Tax Deed and Tax Lien Sales

How long is the redemption period in New York?

Two years after the lien date under Real Property Tax Law section 1110. A tax district may extend it to three or four years for residential or farm property, or cut it to one year for vacant and abandoned residential property.

Do I lose my house the day the redemption period ends?

No. After the period ends the tax district must still win a court judgment, and the notice you receive says you can stay until a court orders you to leave. The notice states the last date to redeem.

Can I get the extra money if my house sells for more than I owe?

Yes, you can file a claim under section 1197 for a share of surplus. For residential property, the proceeding stays open at least three years after the sale report is confirmed if no former homeowner has filed.

What is the difference between a tax lien sale and a tax foreclosure?

A lien sale transfers the right to collect the debt to a purchaser, and you keep the house while you owe the purchaser. A foreclosure ends with a court judgment that transfers ownership of the property to the tax district or its grantee.

Who can I call for free help with property tax arrears?

The homeowner warning notice points to the Attorney General's Homeowner Protection Program hotline, 1-855-HOME-456, and a list of government approved housing counseling agencies in your county. You can also talk to your enforcing officer about a payment plan.
